claim: Electron microscopy (EM) provides a uniquely detailed view of cellular morphology, including organelles and fine subcellular ultrastructure.
source: Electron microscopy (EM) provides a uniquely detailed view of cellular morphology, including organelles and fine subcellular ultrastructure.
evidence: This is a general statement about EM capabilities that draws from established scientific knowledge about the technique.

claim: The acquisition and (semi-)automatic segmentation of multicellular EM volumes are now becoming routine.
source: While the acquisition and (semi-)automatic segmentation of multicellular EM volumes are now becoming routine, large-scale analysis remains severely limited by the lack of generally applicable pipelines for automatic extraction of comprehensive morphological descriptors.
evidence: This statement reflects current trends in the field based on established knowledge of EM technology development.

claim: Large-scale analysis of EM volumes remains severely limited by the lack of generally applicable pipelines for automatic extraction of comprehensive morphological descriptors.
source: While the acquisition and (semi-)automatic segmentation of multicellular EM volumes are now becoming routine, large-scale analysis remains severely limited by the lack of generally applicable pipelines for automatic extraction of comprehensive morphological descriptors.

claim: The authors present a novel unsupervised method for learning cellular morphology features directly from 3D EM data.
source: Here, we present a novel unsupervised method for learning cellular morphology features directly from 3D EM data: a neural network delivers a representation of cells by shape and ultrastructure.
evidence: This is the main methodological contribution described in the abstract.

claim: The neural network delivers a representation of cells by shape and ultrastructure.
source: Here, we present a novel unsupervised method for learning cellular morphology features directly from 3D EM data: a neural network delivers a representation of cells by shape and ultrastructure.
evidence: This describes what the neural network produces as output.

claim: The method was applied to the full volume of an entire three-segmented worm of the annelid Platynereis dumerilii.
source: Applied to the full volume of an entire three-segmented worm of the annelid Platynereis dumerilii, it yields a visually consistent grouping of cells supported by specific gene expression profiles.
evidence: This describes the dataset to which the method was applied.

claim: The method yields a visually consistent grouping of cells supported by specific gene expression profiles.

evidence: This is a key result of applying the method to the Platynereis dataset.

claim: Integration of features across spatial neighbours can retrieve tissues and organs.
source: Integration of features across spatial neighbours can retrieve tissues and organs, revealing, for example, a detailed organisation of the animal foregut.

claim: The method reveals a detailed organisation of the animal foregut.
source: Integration of features across spatial neighbours can retrieve tissues and organs, revealing, for example, a detailed organisation of the animal foregut.

claim: Development of multicellular organisms progressively gives rise to a variety of cell types.
source: Development of multicellular organisms progressively gives rise to a variety of cell types, with differential gene expression resulting in different cellular structures that enable diverse cellular functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about developmental biology based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Differential gene expression results in different cellular structures that enable diverse cellular functions.
source: Development of multicellular organisms progressively gives rise to a variety of cell types, with differential gene expression resulting in different cellular structures that enable diverse cellular functions.
evidence: This describes the relationship between gene expression and cellular structure/function based on established biological knowledge.

claim: Structures and functions together represent the phenotype of an organism.
source: Structures and functions together represent the phenotype of an organism.
evidence: This is a definition based on established biological knowledge.

claim: The characterisation of cell types is important to understand how organisms are built and function in general (Arendt, 2008).
source: The characterisation of cell types is important to understand how organisms are built and function in general (Arendt, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Recent advances in single-cell sequencing have allowed the monitoring of differential gene expression in the cell types that make up the tissues and organs of entire multicellular organisms.
source: Recent advances in single-cell sequencing have allowed the monitoring of differential gene expression in the cell types that make up the tissues and organs of entire multicellular organisms and led to the recognition of distinct regulatory programmes driving the expression of unique sets of cell type-specific effector genes (Hobert and Kratsios, 2019; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2018a; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2018b; Musser et al., 2021; Fincher et al., 2018; Siebert et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to recent work in the field.

claim: Single-cell sequencing has led to the recognition of distinct regulatory programmes driving the expression of unique sets of cell type-specific effector genes (Hobert and Kratsios, 2019; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2018a; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2018b; Musser et al., 2021; Fincher et al., 2018; Siebert et al., 2019).

claim: Distinct genetic programmes make the identity and thus define cell types (Arendt et al., 2016; Tanay and Sebé-Pedrós, 2021).

claim: The rapid progress in volume EM allows imaging of increasingly large samples, including organs and entire smaller animals, with nanometer resolution (Bae et al., 2021; Vergara et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2018; Scheffer et al., 2020; Cook et al., 2019; Verasztó et al., 2020).
source: For the first time, the rapid progress in volume EM allows this for increasingly large samples, including organs and entire smaller animals, with nanometer resolution (Bae et al., 2021; Vergara et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2018; Scheffer et al., 2020; Cook et al., 2019; Verasztó et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement about technological progress is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Automated cell segmentation pipelines support the characterisation and comparison of cellular morphologies (Heinrich et al., 2021; Macrina et al., 2021; Pape et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2021).
source: Supported by automated cell segmentation pipelines (Heinrich et al., 2021; Macrina et al., 2021; Pape et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2021), such datasets allow characterisation and comparison of cellular morphologies, including membrane-bound and membraneless organelles and inclusions, at an unprecedented level of detail for thousands of cells simultaneously (Turner et al., 2022; Vergara et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to segmentation pipeline papers.

claim: EM datasets allow characterisation and comparison of cellular morphologies, including membrane-bound and membraneless organelles and inclusions, at an unprecedented level of detail for thousands of cells simultaneously (Turner et al., 2022; Vergara et al., 2021).
source: Supported by automated cell segmentation pipelines (Heinrich et al., 2021; Macrina et al., 2021; Pape et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2021), such datasets allow characterisation and comparison of cellular morphologies, including membrane-bound and membraneless organelles and inclusions, at an unprecedented level of detail for thousands of cells simultaneously (Turner et al., 2022; Vergara et al., 2021).

claim: The need for automation and quantitative evaluation has triggered the design of complex engineered features that capture specific cell characteristics (Barad et al., 2022).

claim: Manually chosen features often provide only a limited, targeted view of the overall morphology.
source: However, such features often have to be manually chosen and mostly provide only a limited, targeted view of the overall morphology.
evidence: This is a critique of existing methods based on inference from the literature.

claim: Intricate modelling pipelines for cellular morphology quantification have been developed (Ruan et al., 2020; Driscoll et al., 2019; Phillip et al., 2021).
source: To alleviate this problem, intricate modelling pipelines for cellular morphology quantification have been developed (Ruan et al., 2020; Driscoll et al., 2019; Phillip et al., 2021); still, these are often data- and task-specific.

claim: Artificial neural networks have been shown to exceed manually engineered pipelines in extracting comprehensive descriptors for various types of data (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Falk et al., 2019; Simonyan and Zisserman, 2014; Girshick et al., 2014).
source: In the last decade, artificial neural networks have been shown to exceed manually engineered pipelines in extracting comprehensive descriptors for various types of data and to be particularly suited for the extraction of visual features (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Falk et al., 2019; Simonyan and Zisserman, 2014; Girshick et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to deep learning literature.

claim: Neural networks are particularly suited for the extraction of visual features (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Falk et al., 2019; Simonyan and Zisserman, 2014; Girshick et al., 2014).
source: In the last decade, artificial neural networks have been shown to exceed manually engineered pipelines in extracting comprehensive descriptors for various types of data and to be particularly suited for the extraction of visual features (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Falk et al., 2019; Simonyan and Zisserman, 2014; Girshick et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Self-supervised training methods have removed the necessity for generating massive amounts of manual annotations previously needed to train a network.
source: Moreover, the rise of so-called self-supervised training methods has removed the necessity for generating massive amounts of manual annotations previously needed to train a network.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of self-supervised learning based on established knowledge in machine learning.

claim: Self-supervised methods produce descriptors that have been shown to be useful in a variety of downstream tasks, such as image classification, segmentation, and object detection (He et al., 2020; Van den Oord et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2020).
source: Besides the obvious advantage of being less labour-intensive, self-supervised methods do not optimise features for a specific end-task but instead produce descriptors that have been shown to be useful in a variety of downstream tasks, such as image classification, segmentation, and object detection (He et al., 2020; Van den Oord et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to self-supervised learning literature.

claim: Self-supervised methods have shown to be successful for phenotyping cells in image-based profiling (Lu et al., 2019; Lafarge et al., 2019).
source: Such methods have already shown to be successful for phenotyping cells in image-based profiling (Lu et al., 2019; Lafarge et al., 2019) and for describing local morphology of patches or subcompartments within neural cells in 3D electron microscopy (EM) of brain volumes (Huang et al., 2020; Schubert et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Self-supervised methods have been successful for describing local morphology of patches or subcompartments within neural cells in 3D EM of brain volumes (Huang et al., 2020; Schubert et al., 2019).
source: Such methods have already shown to be successful for phenotyping cells in image-based profiling (Lu et al., 2019; Lafarge et al., 2019) and for describing local morphology of patches or subcompartments within neural cells in 3D electron microscopy (EM) of brain volumes (Huang et al., 2020; Schubert et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The authors present the first framework for the fully unsupervised characterisation of cellular shapes and ultrastructures in a whole-body dataset for an entire animal.
source: Here, we present the first framework for the fully unsupervised characterisation of cellular shapes and ultrastructures in a whole-body dataset for an entire animal.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: The method was applied to the fully segmented serial block-face EM (SBEM) volume of the 6 days post fertilisation young worm of the nereid Platynereis dumerilii.
source: We apply this new tool to the fully segmented serial block-face EM (SBEM) volume of the 6 days post fertilisation young worm of the nereid Platynereis dumerilii, comprising 11,402 mostly differentiated cells with distinct morphological properties (Vergara et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: The Platynereis dataset comprises 11,402 mostly differentiated cells with distinct morphological properties (Vergara et al., 2021).
source: We apply this new tool to the fully segmented serial block-face EM (SBEM) volume of the 6 days post fertilisation young worm of the nereid Platynereis dumerilii, comprising 11,402 mostly differentiated cells with distinct morphological properties (Vergara et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the dataset, with citation to the source.

claim: MorphoFeatures are in strong agreement with human perception of morphological similarity.
source: We show that our method yields morphological descriptors - MorphoFeatures - that are in strong agreement with human perception of morphological similarity and quantitatively outperform manually defined features on cell classification and symmetric partner detection tasks.
evidence: This is a result claim based on the experiments performed.

claim: MorphoFeatures quantitatively outperform manually defined features on cell classification and symmetric partner detection tasks.
source: We show that our method yields morphological descriptors - MorphoFeatures - that are in strong agreement with human perception of morphological similarity and quantitatively outperform manually defined features on cell classification and symmetric partner detection tasks.
evidence: This is a quantitative result claim based on experiments.

claim: Similarity-based clustering in the MorphoFeature vector space sorts cells into morphologically meaningful groups that show high correlation with genetically defined types such as muscle cells and neurons.
source: We further illustrate how our features can facilitate the detection of cell types by morphological means, via similarity-based clustering in the MorphoFeature vector space, sorting the cells into morphologically meaningful groups that show high correlation with genetically defined types such as muscle cells and neurons.
evidence: This is a result claim based on clustering analysis and comparison with gene expression data.

claim: The pipeline allows for the characterisation of rare cell types, such as enteric neurons and rhabdomeric photoreceptors.
source: Our pipeline also allows for the characterisation of rare cell types, such as enteric neurons and rhabdomeric photoreceptors, and detects distinct cell populations within the developing midgut.
evidence: This is a result claim based on the analysis performed.

claim: The pipeline detects distinct cell populations within the developing midgut.
source: Our pipeline also allows for the characterisation of rare cell types, such as enteric neurons and rhabdomeric photoreceptors, and detects distinct cell populations within the developing midgut.
evidence: This is a result claim based on the analysis.

claim: MorphoContextFeatures clustering reproduces manually annotated ganglionic nuclei in the annelid brain.
source: We show that such neighbourhood-based MorphoContextFeatures clustering reproduces manually annotated ganglionic nuclei in the annelid brain and represents a powerful tool to automatically and comprehensively detect the distinct tissues that belong to and make up the foregut of the nereid worm - including highly specialised and intricate structures such as the neurosecretory infracerebral gland (Baskin, 1974; Hofmann, 1976; Golding, 1970) and the axochord that has been likened to the chordate notochord (Lauri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a result claim based on comparison with manual annotations.

claim: MorphoContextFeatures can automatically and comprehensively detect the distinct tissues that belong to and make up the foregut of the nereid worm.
source: We show that such neighbourhood-based MorphoContextFeatures clustering reproduces manually annotated ganglionic nuclei in the annelid brain and represents a powerful tool to automatically and comprehensively detect the distinct tissues that belong to and make up the foregut of the nereid worm - including highly specialised and intricate structures such as the neurosecretory infracerebral gland (Baskin, 1974; Hofmann, 1976; Golding, 1970) and the axochord that has been likened to the chordate notochord (Lauri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a result claim based on the analysis performed.

claim: The foregut includes highly specialised structures such as the neurosecretory infracerebral gland (Baskin, 1974; Hofmann, 1976; Golding, 1970).

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The axochord has been likened to the chordate notochord (Lauri et al., 2014).

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Morphologically defined tissues and organs correlate with cell type and tissue-specific gene expression.
source: We further show that such morphologically defined tissues and organs correlate with cell type and tissue-specific gene expression.
evidence: This is a result claim based on comparison with gene expression data.

claim: The pipeline requires prior segmentation of all the cells and nuclei of interest.
source: Our pipeline has been designed to extract morphological descriptors of cells (MorphoFeatures) from EM data. It requires prior segmentation of all the cells and nuclei of interest.
evidence: This describes a requirement of the method.

claim: The pipeline represents cell morphology as a combination of three essential components: shape, coarse, and fine texture.
source: The pipeline utilises segmentation masks to extract single cells/nuclei and represents their morphology as a combination of three essential components: shape, coarse, and fine texture (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the design of the method, with reference to a figure.

claim: Neural networks are trained to represent shape, coarse texture, and fine texture components independently.
source: We train neural networks to represent these components independently, using point clouds as input for shape, low-resolution raw data for coarse texture with sufficient context and small, high-resolution crops of raw data for fine texture.
evidence: This describes the training approach.

claim: Point clouds are used as input for shape features.
source: We train neural networks to represent these components independently, using point clouds as input for shape, low-resolution raw data for coarse texture with sufficient context and small, high-resolution crops of raw data for fine texture.
evidence: This describes the input representation for shape.

claim: Low-resolution raw data is used for coarse texture features.
source: We train neural networks to represent these components independently, using point clouds as input for shape, low-resolution raw data for coarse texture with sufficient context and small, high-resolution crops of raw data for fine texture.
evidence: This describes the input for coarse texture.

claim: Small, high-resolution crops of raw data are used for fine texture features.
source: We train neural networks to represent these components independently, using point clouds as input for shape, low-resolution raw data for coarse texture with sufficient context and small, high-resolution crops of raw data for fine texture.
evidence: This describes the input for fine texture.

claim: Separating morphological components ensures they are all represented in the final features and facilitates further interpretation.
source: Separating these components ensures they are all represented in the final features and facilitates further interpretation.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the design choice.

claim: The features are combined to form one feature vector for each cell of the animal.
source: The features are combined to form one feature vector for each cell of the animal.
evidence: This describes how the final feature vector is constructed.

claim: The training pipeline is based on two complementary objectives: an autoencoder reconstruction loss and a contrastive loss.
source: To enable immediate data exploration even for datasets where direct supervision is hard to define and the ground truth cannot easily be obtained, we developed a fully unsupervised training pipeline that is based on two complementary objectives (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This describes the training methodology with reference to figures.

claim: The autoencoder reconstruction loss encourages the network to extract the most comprehensive description.
source: The first is an autoencoder reconstruction loss, where a network extracts a low-dimensional representation of each cell and then uses this representation to reconstruct back the original cell volume. This loss encourages the network to extract the most comprehensive description.
evidence: This explains the purpose of the autoencoder loss.

claim: The contrastive loss ensures the feature vectors extracted from two similarly looking cells are closer to each other than to feature vectors extracted from more dissimilar cells.
source: The second objective is a contrastive loss that ensures the feature vectors extracted from two similarly looking cells (positive samples) are closer to each other than to feature vectors extracted from more dissimilar cells (negative samples).
evidence: This explains the purpose of the contrastive loss.

claim: Positive samples are generated by applying realistic transformations to cell volumes.
source: Since we do not know in advance which samples can be considered positive for our dataset, we are using slightly different views of the same cell, generated by applying realistic transformations to cell volumes (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes how positive samples are created for contrastive learning.

claim: The combination of autoencoder and contrastive losses encourages the learned features to retain the maximal amount of information about the cells while enforcing distances between feature vectors to reflect morphological similarity.
source: The combination of these two losses encourages the learned features to retain the maximal amount of information about the cells, while enforcing distances between feature vectors to reflect morphological similarity of cells.
evidence: This explains the combined effect of the two losses.

claim: The Platynereis atlas comprises a 3D SBEM volume of the whole animal with sufficient resolution to distinguish ultrastructural elements.
source: The pipeline was trained and applied on the cellular atlas of the marine annelid P. dumerilii (Vergara et al., 2021). It comprises a 3D SBEM volume of the whole animal that has sufficient resolution to distinguish ultrastructural elements (organelles and inclusions, nuclear and cytoplasm texture, etc.) and an automated segmentation of 11,402 cells and nuclei (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the dataset used, with citation.

claim: The Platynereis atlas includes an automated segmentation of 11,402 cells and nuclei.
source: The pipeline was trained and applied on the cellular atlas of the marine annelid P. dumerilii (Vergara et al., 2021). It comprises a 3D SBEM volume of the whole animal that has sufficient resolution to distinguish ultrastructural elements (organelles and inclusions, nuclear and cytoplasm texture, etc.) and an automated segmentation of 11,402 cells and nuclei (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the dataset, with citation.

claim: Whole-animal gene expression maps are available for Platynereis that cover many differentiation genes and transcription factors.
source: Additionally, whole-animal gene expression maps are available that cover many differentiation genes and transcription factors.
evidence: This describes additional data available for the organism.

claim: The training procedure yields 480 features that describe each cell in terms of its cytoplasm and nucleus shape, coarse texture, and fine texture.
source: We designed MorphoFeatures to enable unbiased exploration of morphological variability in the animal on both cellular and tissue level; and indeed our training procedure yields 480 features that extensively describe each cell in terms of its cytoplasm and nucleus shape, coarse texture, and fine texture (80 features for each category).
evidence: This describes the output of the training procedure.

claim: Each morphological category (shape, coarse texture, fine texture for cytoplasm and nucleus) is represented by 80 features.
source: We designed MorphoFeatures to enable unbiased exploration of morphological variability in the animal on both cellular and tissue level; and indeed our training procedure yields 480 features that extensively describe each cell in terms of its cytoplasm and nucleus shape, coarse texture, and fine texture (80 features for each category).
evidence: This specifies the dimensionality of each feature component.

claim: A logistic regression classifier trained on MorphoFeatures achieved an accuracy of 96% on predicting seven morphological cell classes.
source: A classifier with MorphoFeatures achieved an accuracy of 96%, showing that the learned features are sufficient to distinguish broad morphological classes.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the classification experiment.

claim: The classifier tends to confuse some secretory cells with other types (midgut and epithelial cells) that are also difficult to discern by eye.
source: This reveals, as expected, that while morphologically homogeneous classes can be easily separated, the classifier tends to confuse some secretory cells with other types (midgut and epithelial cells) that are also difficult to discern by eye and might well be mis-annotated.
evidence: This is an analysis of the classification errors.

claim: The classifier confuses the general neuron class with neurosecretory cells that represent a subclass of neurons.
source: It also confuses the general neuron class with neurosecretory cells that represent a subclass of neurons.
evidence: This is an analysis of classification errors.

claim: The model successfully predicted cells outlining the gut opening and the chaetae cells as epithelial, even though it was trained exclusively on cells of the outer animal surface.
source: These results demonstrate that MorphoFeatures are sufficiently expressive to enable training a generalisable model from a small number of labels, taking epithelial cells as a showcase: while the model was trained exclusively on the cells of the outer animal surface, it successfully predicted the cells outlining the gut opening and the chaetae cells as epithelial as well.
evidence: This demonstrates the generalization capability of the model.

claim: The model predicted some cells in the midgut region as neurons, which were confirmed to be enteric neurons after visual examination.
source: Even more convincingly, the model predicted some cells in the midgut region as neurons, which after careful visual examination were indeed confirmed to be enteric neurons.
evidence: This demonstrates the model's ability to detect rare cell types.

claim: Cytoplasm texture is sufficient to distinguish some cell classes with high precision.
source: The results show that, for example, cytoplasm texture is sufficient to tell some classes apart with high precision.
evidence: This is a result from the component analysis experiment.

claim: Both coarse and fine cytoplasm texture perform slightly worse on distinguishing neurosecretory cells, in which nuclei occupy almost the whole cell volume.
source: However, both coarse and fine cytoplasm texture perform slightly worse on distinguishing neurosecretory cells, in which nuclei occupy almost the whole cell volume.
evidence: This is a result from the component analysis with an explanation.

claim: Cell shape is satisfactory to characterise neurons and muscle cells but shows inferior performance on epithelial and secretory cells, which display a great variety of cell shapes.
source: Cell shape is satisfactory to characterise neurons and muscle cells but shows inferior performance on epithelial and secretory cells, which display a great variety of cell shapes.
evidence: This is a result from the component analysis with an explanation.

claim: Nuclear fine texture features correctly distinguish muscle cells, suggesting that this class has characteristic chromatin texture.
source: Surprisingly, nuclear fine texture features correctly distinguish, among other classes, muscle cells, suggesting that this class has characteristic chromatin texture.
evidence: This is a result with an interpretation.

claim: Manually defined features from Vergara et al., 2021 achieved an accuracy of 94% on the same classification task.
source: In Vergara et al., 2021, morphological classification of cells was performed based on manually defined features, including descriptors of shape (e.g. volume, sphericity, and major and minor axes), intensity (e.g. intensity mean, median and SD), and texture (Haralick features) extracted from the cell, nucleus, and chromatin segmentations, with 140 features in total. To compare these explicitly defined features with implicitly learned MorphoFeatures, we passed them through the same evaluation pipeline yielding a classifier which achieves the accuracy of 94%, in comparison to 96% achieved by MorphoFeatures.
evidence: This is a comparison result with the baseline method.

claim: MorphoFeatures are 38% more precise in locating a symmetric partner than manually defined features from Vergara et al., 2021.
source: According to this metric, our MorphoFeatures are 38% more precise in locating a symmetric partner than the ones from Vergara et al., 2021, showing the widely accepted superiority of neural network extracted features to explicitly defined ones.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison result.

claim: Cells in close proximity in the MorphoFeature space appear highly visually similar and might represent cell types at the morphological level.
source: This shows that cells in close proximity in the feature space appear highly visually similar and might represent cell types at the morphological level.
evidence: This is an observation from the UMAP visualization analysis.

claim: A group of secretory cells with cytoplasm filled with round electron-transparent vesicles corresponds to the 'bright droplets' cells from Verasztó et al., 2020.
source: For example, a group of secretory cells in which the cytoplasm is filled with round electron-transparent vesicles (upper green panel) corresponds to the 'bright droplets' cells from Verasztó et al., 2020.
evidence: This identifies a specific cell group with reference to previous literature.

claim: A group of secretory cells with extensive endoplasmic reticulum surrounding the nucleus represents parapodial spinning gland cells (Verasztó et al., 2020).
source: Another group of secretory cells has an extensive endoplasmic reticulum (ER) surrounding the nucleus with a prominent nucleolus (lower green panel) and represents parapodial spinning gland cells (Verasztó et al., 2020).
evidence: This identifies a specific cell group with citation.

claim: Neurons show remarkable diversity based on soma morphology only, even though neurite morphology is not taken into account.
source: Another interesting observation is that even though the neurite morphology is not taken into account, neurons show remarkable diversity based on soma morphology only (blue panels).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis.

claim: A group of cells initially labelled as neurons that are located next to epithelial cells on the UMAP projection are sensory cells that extend their processes to the epithelial surface.
source: Careful examination of a group of cells, initially labelled as neurons, that are located next to the epithelial cells on the UMAP projection (upper right blue panel) revealed that these cells are sensory cells that extend their processes to the epithelial surface.
evidence: This is a discovery made through the analysis.

claim: Hierarchical clustering split cells into 15 broad morphological groups.
source: To explore the structure of the MorphoFeatures space, we performed hierarchical clustering of all cells. In the first clustering round, we split cells into 15 broad morphological groups (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the clustering result.

claim: Clusters 1–8 represent different groups of neurons.
source: Cluster content could be revealed through available annotations and visualisation with the PlatyBrowser (Pape et al., 2022; Figure 3B): Clusters 1–8 represent different groups of neurons; 9–11 epithelial cells; 12 and 13 are muscles; 14 midgut cells; while cluster 15 was further subclustered into secretory cells (subcluster 1) and ciliary band cells (subcluster 2).
evidence: This describes the cluster identities.

claim: Clusters 9–11 represent epithelial cells.
source: Cluster content could be revealed through available annotations and visualisation with the PlatyBrowser (Pape et al., 2022; Figure 3B): Clusters 1–8 represent different groups of neurons; 9–11 epithelial cells; 12 and 13 are muscles; 14 midgut cells; while cluster 15 was further subclustered into secretory cells (subcluster 1) and ciliary band cells (subcluster 2).
evidence: This describes the cluster identities.

claim: Clusters 12 and 13 are muscles.
source: Cluster content could be revealed through available annotations and visualisation with the PlatyBrowser (Pape et al., 2022; Figure 3B): Clusters 1–8 represent different groups of neurons; 9–11 epithelial cells; 12 and 13 are muscles; 14 midgut cells; while cluster 15 was further subclustered into secretory cells (subcluster 1) and ciliary band cells (subcluster 2).
evidence: This describes the cluster identities.

claim: Cluster 14 represents midgut cells.
source: Cluster content could be revealed through available annotations and visualisation with the PlatyBrowser (Pape et al., 2022; Figure 3B): Clusters 1–8 represent different groups of neurons; 9–11 epithelial cells; 12 and 13 are muscles; 14 midgut cells; while cluster 15 was further subclustered into secretory cells (subcluster 1) and ciliary band cells (subcluster 2).
evidence: This describes the cluster identities.

claim: Cluster 15 was further subclustered into secretory cells (subcluster 1) and ciliary band cells (subcluster 2).
source: Cluster content could be revealed through available annotations and visualisation with the PlatyBrowser (Pape et al., 2022; Figure 3B): Clusters 1–8 represent different groups of neurons; 9–11 epithelial cells; 12 and 13 are muscles; 14 midgut cells; while cluster 15 was further subclustered into secretory cells (subcluster 1) and ciliary band cells (subcluster 2).
evidence: This describes the subclustering result.

claim: Foregut epithelial cells are distinct from the epithelial cells of the outer animal surface and chaetae cells (clusters 9, 11, and 10, respectively).
source: For example, the foregut epithelial cells are distinct from the epithelial cells of the outer animal surface and chaetae cells (clusters 9, 11, and 10, respectively).
evidence: This describes a specific finding from the clustering.

claim: Foregut neurons form a separate cluster (cluster 4).
source: Separate groups are also formed by different types of neurons, for example, foregut neurons (cluster 4).
evidence: This describes a specific cluster.

claim: Cluster 5 shows specific expression of Trp channels pkd2, trpV4, and trpV5, and the bHLH transcription factor asci, which demarcate sensory cells of the palpal, antennal, and cirral ganglia (Vergara et al., 2021).
source: Among the neurons, cluster 5 shows the most specific gene expression including the Transient receptor potential (Trp) channels pkd2, trpV4, and trpV5, and the bHLH transcription factor asci, which demarcate sensory cells of the palpal, antennal, and cirral ganglia (Vergara et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes gene expression patterns for a specific cluster with citation.

claim: Cluster 1 shows specific expression of the homeodomain transcription factors lhx6 and phox2 and an ap2 family member.
source: Cluster 1 shows specific expression of the homeodomain transcription factors lhx6 and phox2 and an ap2 family member, while cluster 6 composed of dark neurosecretory cells shows specific expression of two neurosecretion markers, atrial natriuretic peptide receptor anpra and prohormone convertase phc2, identifying these as brain parts of the circular and apical nervous system, respectively (Vergara et al., 2021; Arendt, 2021).
evidence: This describes gene expression for a specific cluster.

claim: Cluster 6 composed of dark neurosecretory cells shows specific expression of atrial natriuretic peptide receptor anpra and prohormone convertase phc2, identifying these as brain parts of the circular and apical nervous system (Vergara et al., 2021; Arendt, 2021).
source: Cluster 1 shows specific expression of the homeodomain transcription factors lhx6 and phox2 and an ap2 family member, while cluster 6 composed of dark neurosecretory cells shows specific expression of two neurosecretion markers, atrial natriuretic peptide receptor anpra and prohormone convertase phc2, identifying these as brain parts of the circular and apical nervous system, respectively (Vergara et al., 2021; Arendt, 2021).
evidence: This describes gene expression and identity of a cluster with citations.

claim: Cluster 8 is enriched for the oxidative stress marker cytoglobin (globin-like; Song et al., 2020) and the bHLH transcription factor mitf.
source: Cluster 8, another neural cluster, is enriched for the oxidative stress marker cytoglobin (globin-like; Song et al., 2020) and the bHLH transcription factor mitf.
evidence: This describes gene expression for a cluster with citation.

claim: Subcluster 8.1 represents rhabdomeric photoreceptors of the adult eye that specifically express mitf and globin-like.
source: Subclustering revealed three subclusters, one of which represents rhabdomeric photoreceptors of the adult eye (Figure 3B, subcluster 8.1) that specifically express mitf and globin-like.
evidence: This identifies a specific subcluster and its gene expression.

claim: An average cell in subcluster 8.1 shows abundant black inclusions.
source: An average cell in this subcluster (Figure 4B) shows abundant black inclusions.
evidence: This describes the morphology of cells in the subcluster with reference to a figure.

claim: Subcluster 8.2 contains pigment cells with black pigment granules.
source: The second subcluster (8.2) contains pigment cells with black pigment granules.
evidence: This identifies a subcluster.

claim: Cells in subcluster 8.3 are located in the midgut, with a smooth oval shape, neurite extensions and nuclei taking up the most cell volume, making it likely that these cells represent enteric neurons previously postulated on the basis of serotonin staining (Brunet et al., 2016).
source: Cells in the third subcluster (8.3) are located in the midgut, with a smooth oval shape, neurite extensions and nuclei taking up the most cell volume (Figure 4C and D) - in striking contrast to other midgut cells but resembling neurons, making it likely that these cells represent enteric neurons previously postulated on the basis of serotonin staining (Brunet et al., 2016).
evidence: This identifies a subcluster and interprets its identity with citation.

claim: The outer epithelial cluster 11 is enriched for protocadherin (pcdh15) and neurotrypsin (ntrps).
source: Among the epidermal cells, the outer cluster 11 is enriched for protocadherin (pcdh15) and neurotrypsin (ntrps), whereas cluster 9 representing foregut epidermis shows high specificity for the bHLH transcription factor sim1 and the homeodomain factor pou3 (brn124, known to be expressed in stomodeal ectoderm in sea urchin; Cole and Arnone, 2009).
evidence: This describes gene expression for a cluster.

claim: Cluster 9 representing foregut epidermis shows high specificity for the bHLH transcription factor sim1 and the homeodomain factor pou3 (brn124, known to be expressed in stomodeal ectoderm in sea urchin; Cole and Arnone, 2009).
source: Among the epidermal cells, the outer cluster 11 is enriched for protocadherin (pcdh15) and neurotrypsin (ntrps), whereas cluster 9 representing foregut epidermis shows high specificity for the bHLH transcription factor sim1 and the homeodomain factor pou3 (brn124, known to be expressed in stomodeal ectoderm in sea urchin; Cole and Arnone, 2009).
evidence: This describes gene expression for a cluster with citation.

claim: The specific expression of striated muscle-specific myosin heavy chain mhcl4 in cluster 12 denotes the group of striated somatic muscles.
source: For the muscles, the specific expression of striated muscle-specific myosin heavy chain mhcl4 in cluster 12 denotes the group of striated somatic muscles, while its absence in cluster 13 indicates that the foregut muscles have not yet switched to expressing striated markers (Brunet et al., 2016).
evidence: This interprets gene expression to identify muscle type.

claim: The absence of mhcl4 in cluster 13 indicates that the foregut muscles have not yet switched to expressing striated markers (Brunet et al., 2016).
source: For the muscles, the specific expression of striated muscle-specific myosin heavy chain mhcl4 in cluster 12 denotes the group of striated somatic muscles, while its absence in cluster 13 indicates that the foregut muscles have not yet switched to expressing striated markers (Brunet et al., 2016).
evidence: This interprets gene expression with citation.

claim: Cluster 13 shows high and specific expression of calexcitin-like sarcoplasmic calcium-binding protein Scp2 (calexcitin2; White et al., 2011), calmodulin, and Boule homologue Boll (boule-like).
source: Instead, the high and specific expression of the calexcitin-like sarcoplasmic calcium-binding protein Scp2 (calexcitin2; White et al., 2011), calmodulin, and of the Boule homologue Boll (boule-like) in cluster 13 suggests a calcium excitation and/or sequestration mechanism specific for foregut muscles.
evidence: This describes gene expression with citation.

claim: The gene expression pattern in cluster 13 suggests a calcium excitation and/or sequestration mechanism specific for foregut muscles.
source: Instead, the high and specific expression of the calexcitin-like sarcoplasmic calcium-binding protein Scp2 (calexcitin2; White et al., 2011), calmodulin, and of the Boule homologue Boll (boule-like) in cluster 13 suggests a calcium excitation and/or sequestration mechanism specific for foregut muscles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of gene expression data.

claim: The midgut cluster (cluster 14) specifically expresses the forkhead domain transcription factor foxA (for), a gut developmental marker (Boyle and Seaver, 2008).
source: Finally, the cluster of midgut cells (cluster 14) specifically expresses the forkhead domain transcription factor foxA (for), a gut developmental marker (Boyle and Seaver, 2008) and TrpV-c, another Trp channel paralogue of the vanilloid subtype with presumed mechanosensory function.
evidence: This describes gene expression with citation.

claim: The midgut cluster specifically expresses TrpV-c, a Trp channel paralogue of the vanilloid subtype with presumed mechanosensory function.
source: Finally, the cluster of midgut cells (cluster 14) specifically expresses the forkhead domain transcription factor foxA (for), a gut developmental marker (Boyle and Seaver, 2008) and TrpV-c, another Trp channel paralogue of the vanilloid subtype with presumed mechanosensory function.
evidence: This describes gene expression with functional speculation.

claim: Finer clustering of the midgut cluster revealed one subcluster with strong expression of smooth muscle markers non-muscle-mhc and mrlc2.
source: Finer clustering (Figure 5) revealed one subcluster with strong expression of the smooth muscle markers non-muscle-mhc and mrlc2, and another expressing a chitinase related to chitotriosidase (nov2) and the zinc finger transcription factor Prdm16/mecom, known to maintain homeostasis in intestinal epithelia (Stine et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a subclustering result and gene expression.

claim: Another midgut subcluster expresses a chitinase related to chitotriosidase (nov2) and the zinc finger transcription factor Prdm16/mecom, known to maintain homeostasis in intestinal epithelia (Stine et al., 2019).
source: Finer clustering (Figure 5) revealed one subcluster with strong expression of the smooth muscle markers non-muscle-mhc and mrlc2, and another expressing a chitinase related to chitotriosidase (nov2) and the zinc finger transcription factor Prdm16/mecom, known to maintain homeostasis in intestinal epithelia (Stine et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes gene expression with citation.

claim: The midgut subclusters represent distinct territories in the differentiating midgut, interpreted as midgut smooth musculature and digestive epithelia.
source: Visualising the cells belonging to each subcluster and the specifically expressed genes in the PlatyBrowser (Figure 5E) revealed distinct territories in the differentiating midgut, which we interpret as midgut smooth musculature and digestive epithelia.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the clustering and gene expression results.

claim: A third midgut-like cluster is located outside of the midgut, in the animal parapodia, comprising cells that resemble midgut cells morphologically.
source: We also detected an enigmatic third cluster located outside of the midgut, in the animal parapodia, comprising cells that resemble midgut cells morphologically (Figure 5D).
evidence: This describes a discovery from the analysis.

claim: For the third midgut-like cluster, the current gene repertoire did not reveal any specifically expressed gene.
source: For this subcluster, the current gene repertoire of the cellular expression atlas did not reveal any specifically expressed gene.
evidence: This describes a limitation in the gene expression data.

claim: Many MorphoFeatures can be matched to visually comprehensible properties.
source: Visual inspection showed that many of them can be matched to visually comprehensible properties.
evidence: This is a result from the feature interpretability analysis.

claim: Cytoplasm coarse texture feature 21 distinguishes outer epithelial cells (cluster 11).
source: For example, cytoplasm coarse texture feature 21 (Figure 6, upper left), which distinguishes the outer epithelial cells (cluster 11), shows its minimal value in secretory cells, which contain multiple highly distinct types of texture, and its maximal value in the cells crowded with small vesicles and cisternae on the surface of the animal.
evidence: This describes a specific feature and its interpretation.

claim: Nuclear coarse texture feature 4 distinguishes the cluster of enteric neurons (cluster 8.3) from other neurons.
source: The cluster of enteric neurons (cluster 8.3) strongly differs from other neurons by nuclear coarse texture feature 4 (Figure 6, upper right), which contrasts nuclei with large amount of heterochromatin often attached to the nuclear lamina to nuclei with a high amount of euchromatin and prominent nucleoli.
evidence: This describes a specific feature and its interpretation.

claim: Cytoplasm fine texture feature 50 is characteristic of midgut cells (cluster 14).
source: Cytoplasm fine texture feature 50 (Figure 6, middle left), characteristic to the midgut cells (cluster 14), is the lowest in cells with a small stretch of homogeneous cytoplasm with mitochondria and has its peak in cells with abundant Golgi cisternae and medium-sized mitochondria.
evidence: This describes a specific feature and its interpretation.

claim: Rhabdomeric photoreceptors (cluster 8.1) display specific nuclear fine texture feature 7 that differentiates between nuclei with smooth and rather grainy texture.
source: Rhabdomeric photoreceptors of the adult eye (cluster 8.1) display specific nuclear fine texture feature 7 (Figure 6, middle right) that differentiates between nuclei with smooth and rather grainy texture.
evidence: This describes a specific feature.

claim: Cell shape feature 14 is specific for ciliary band cells (cluster 15.2).
source: Cell shape feature 14 (Figure 6, lower left) has its minimal value found in beaker-shaped cells with smooth surface and its maximal value in rather round cells with extremely rugged surface and is specific for ciliary band cells (cluster 15.2).
evidence: This describes a specific feature.

claim: Foregut muscles (cluster 13) can be described using nuclear shape feature 66.
source: Foregut muscles (cluster 13) can be described using nuclear shape feature 66 (Figure 6, lower right), having one extreme in nuclei with a small compartment with a rough surface (as a result of a segmentation error) and the other extreme in elongated flat nuclei.
evidence: This describes a specific feature.

claim: MorphoContextFeatures are created by combining the MorphoFeatures of a cell with the average MorphoFeatures of its immediate neighbours.
source: For this, we combined the MorphoFeatures of a cell with the average MorphoFeatures of its immediate neighbours, yielding a feature vector that represents the morphology of both the cell and its surrounding, which we refer to as MorphoContextFeatures.
evidence: This describes how MorphoContextFeatures are constructed.

claim: Proximity in MorphoContextFeature space identifies neighbouring groups of morphologically similar cells.
source: Applying the representation analysis described before, we find that proximity in MorphoContextFeature space no longer reflects morphological similarity only but rather identifies neighbouring groups of morphologically similar cells (whereby the neighbouring groups can be morphologically dissimilar).
evidence: This describes what MorphoContextFeatures capture.

claim: MorphoContextFeatures identify different tissues that together constitute organs composed of various tissues.
source: In other words, we now identify different tissues that together constitute organs composed of various tissues (Figure 7).
evidence: This describes the capability of MorphoContextFeatures.

claim: A separate assembly of groups of cells in the lower part of the UMAP projection represents the animal foregut subdivided into its constituting tissues.
source: For example, a separate assembly of groups of cells in the lower part of the UMAP projection represents the animal foregut subdivided into its constituting tissues comprising foregut neurons (lower blue panel), foregut muscles (lower beige panel), and foregut epithelium (left yellow-green panel).
evidence: This describes a specific finding from the MorphoContextFeatures analysis.

claim: Adding neighbourhood information helps distinguish cirral, palpal, and dorsal ganglia, as well as the ventral nerve cord and peripheral ganglia.
source: For the nervous system, adding neighbourhood information helps distinguishing cirral, palpal, and dorsal ganglia (three upper right panels, from left to right), as well as the ventral nerve cord and peripheral ganglia (two lower right panels).
evidence: This describes the benefit of neighborhood information.

claim: MorphoContextFeature clustering was compared to both manually segmented ganglionic nuclei and genetically defined neuronal clusters.
source: To benchmark the quality of this grouping, we clustered all the cells in the MorphoContextFeature space (see Materials and methods) and compared the neuron clusters to both manually segmented ganglionic nuclei and to the genetically defined neuronal clusters taking into account available gene expression in the cellular atlas (Vergara et al., 2021; Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This describes the benchmarking approach.

claim: Manual segmentation of brain tissues has lower quality in areas where tissue boundaries are not sufficiently distinct.
source: Notably, manual segmentation of brain tissues relied on visible tissue boundaries and thus has lower quality in the areas where such boundaries are not sufficiently distinct.
evidence: This is a critique of the manual segmentation baseline.

claim: All three ways of defining ganglia (manual segmentation, MorphoContextFeature clustering, and gene clustering) lead to very similar results.
source: In essence, all three ways of defining ganglia lead to very similar results (Figure 8B), yet MorphoContextFeature clustering appeared to be the most powerful.
evidence: This is a comparison result.

claim: MorphoContextFeature clustering appeared to be the most powerful method for defining ganglia.
source: In essence, all three ways of defining ganglia lead to very similar results (Figure 8B), yet MorphoContextFeature clustering appeared to be the most powerful.
evidence: This is a comparative evaluation.

claim: Gene clustering failed to distinguish the circumpalpal ganglion due to the lack of distinct gene expression in the atlas.
source: Gene clustering failed to distinguish the circumpalpal ganglion, defined both by manual segmentation and MorphoContextFeature clustering, due to the lack of distinct gene expression in the atlas.
evidence: This describes a limitation of gene-based clustering.

claim: Manual segmentation failed to distinguish between the dorso-posterior and dorsal-anterior ganglionic nuclei due to the lack of distinct tissue boundaries.
source: Manual segmentation failed to distinguish between the dorso-posterior and dorsal-anterior ganglionic nuclei due to the lack of distinct tissue boundaries.
evidence: This describes a limitation of manual segmentation.

claim: The dorso-posterior and dorsal-anterior ganglionic nuclei are well defined by gene clustering and subdivided even further by MorphoContextFeature clustering.
source: These are well defined by gene clustering and subdivided even further by MorphoContextFeature clustering.
evidence: This describes the advantage of MorphoContextFeature clustering.

claim: MorphoContextFeatures sometimes led to ambiguous assignment of cells neighbouring other tissues, especially cells with strongly different morphology.
source: Unaware of the physical tissue boundaries, MorphoContextFeatures sometimes led to ambiguous assignment of cells neighbouring other tissues, especially cells with strongly different morphology.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the method.

claim: Subclustering of the foregut region revealed various foregut tissues including foregut epidermis, ganglia, inner musculature, and a prominent muscle surrounding the foregut.
source: To further illustrate how MorphoContextFeatures can assist an unbiased exploration of an animal EM volume, we focused on the foregut. Subclustering whenever suitable (Figure 9A; see Materials and methods), the resulting clusters revealed various foregut tissues including foregut epidermis, ganglia, inner musculature, and a prominent muscle surrounding the foregut.
evidence: This describes the results of foregut analysis.

claim: A tissue of secretory neuron-like cells surrounds the foregut like a collar.
source: We also found a tissue of secretory neuron-like cells that surround the foregut like a collar (Figure 9B and C, in green).
evidence: This describes a specific tissue discovered.

claim: The secretory neuron-like structure is located underneath the brain neuropil and close to the neurosecretory endings of the neurosecretory plexus (Verasztó et al., 2020).
source: Further inspection revealed that the latter structure is located underneath the brain neuropil and close to the neurosecretory endings of the neurosecretory plexus (Verasztó et al., 2020) and is bounded by thin layers of longitudinal muscle fibres on both the outer and the inner surface (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes the location of the structure with citation.

claim: The secretory structure is bounded by thin layers of longitudinal muscle fibres on both the outer and the inner surface.
source: Further inspection revealed that the latter structure is located underneath the brain neuropil and close to the neurosecretory endings of the neurosecretory plexus (Verasztó et al., 2020) and is bounded by thin layers of longitudinal muscle fibres on both the outer and the inner surface (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes the structure.

claim: The location of the structure indicated it might be the differentiating infracerebral gland - a neurosecretory gland located beneath the brain assumed to play a role in sensing blood glucose levels (Backfisch, 2013; Baskin, 1974; Hofmann, 1976; Golding, 1970).
source: The location of the structure indicated it might be the differentiating infracerebral gland - a neurosecretory gland located beneath the brain assumed to play a role in sensing blood glucose levels (Backfisch, 2013; Baskin, 1974; Hofmann, 1976; Golding, 1970).
evidence: This is an interpretation with citations to previous literature.

claim: The organ is leaf-shaped and lays between the posterior pair of adult eyes as described in Backfisch, 2013.
source: The organ is leaf-shaped and lays between the posterior pair of adult eyes (Figure 9—figure supplement 2B) as also described in Backfisch, 2013 and borders a cavity likely to be a developing blood vessel (Figure 9—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This describes the structure with citation.

claim: The infracerebral gland borders a cavity likely to be a developing blood vessel.
source: The organ is leaf-shaped and lays between the posterior pair of adult eyes (Figure 9—figure supplement 2B) as also described in Backfisch, 2013 and borders a cavity likely to be a developing blood vessel (Figure 9—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structure.

claim: In comparison to the foregut neurons that express sodium channel scn8aa, the infracerebral gland cells specifically express homeobox protein onecut/hnf6.
source: In comparison to the foregut neurons that express sodium channel scn8aa, the infracerebral gland cells specifically express homeobox protein onecut/hnf6 (Figure 9D and E).
evidence: This describes differential gene expression.

claim: The infracerebral gland tissue stains positive for EdU applied between 3 and 5 dpf, indicating that it is still proliferating.
source: We also noted that the tissue stains positive for EdU applied between 3 and 5 dpf, indicating that it is still proliferating.
evidence: This is an observation with interpretation.

claim: The prominent muscles surrounding the foregut were identified as the anterior extension of the axochord (Lauri et al., 2014).
source: We then identified the prominent muscles surrounding the foregut as the anterior extension of the axochord (Lauri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an identification with citation.

claim: The axochord muscles show specific expression of type I collagen gene col1a1, a marker for axochordal tissue.
source: Visualising the genes specifically expressed in these muscles, we noticed specific expression of the type I collagen gene col1a1, a marker for axochordal tissue, and of muscle junctional gene junctophilin1 (Figure 9F).
evidence: This describes gene expression.

claim: The axochord muscles show specific expression of muscle junctional gene junctophilin1.
source: Visualising the genes specifically expressed in these muscles, we noticed specific expression of the type I collagen gene col1a1, a marker for axochordal tissue, and of muscle junctional gene junctophilin1 (Figure 9F).
evidence: This describes gene expression.

claim: An anterior extension of the axochord around the foregut has been observed in several species and is described in Lauri et al., 2014; Brunet et al., 2016; Nielsen et al., 2018.
source: An anterior extension of the axochord around the foregut has been observed in several species and is described in Lauri et al., 2014; Brunet et al., 2016; Nielsen et al., 2018.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The obtained MorphoFeatures capture fine morphological peculiarities and group together cells with similar visual appearance and localisation in the animal.
source: We train a deep-learning pipeline optimised for these two conditions and show that it produces rich cellular representations, combining shape-, ultrastructure-, and texture-based features. More precisely, we show that the obtained representations (MorphoFeatures) capture fine morphological peculiarities and group together cells with similar visual appearance and localisation in the animal.
evidence: This is a summary of results.

claim: Clustering of cells in the MorphoFeature space shows that the obtained clusters represent units with differential and coherent gene expression.
source: Clustering of cells in the MorphoFeature space and taking advantage of an existing gene expression atlas with cellular resolution, we show that the obtained clusters represent units with differential and coherent gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary of results.

claim: MorphoFeatures can facilitate unbiased exploratory analysis aimed at detecting and characterising unusual phenotypes or unusual cell neighbourhoods.
source: Both for morphological type and for tissue detection, we illustrate how MorphoFeatures can facilitate unbiased exploratory analysis aimed at detecting and characterising unusual phenotypes or unusual cell neighbourhoods.
evidence: This describes a capability of the method.

claim: MorphoFeatures show quantitative superiority over manually defined features on the tasks of cell classification and symmetric partner detection.
source: Moreover, we show quantitative superiority of MorphoFeatures over a broad range of manually defined features on the tasks of cell classification and symmetric partner detection.
evidence: This is a summary of quantitative results.

claim: Despite being learned implicitly, MorphoFeatures still correspond to visually understandable properties and can often be interpreted.
source: We also show that, despite being learned implicitly, MorphoFeatures still correspond to visually understandable properties and can often be interpreted.
evidence: This is a summary of the interpretability analysis.

claim: MorphoContextFeatures reveal the power of the approach to detect local groups of cells with similar morphology that represent tissues.
source: Finally, adding morphological information from the neighbouring cells (MorphoContextFeatures), we reveal the power of our approach to detect local groups of cells with similar morphology that represent tissues.
evidence: This is a summary of the neighborhood-based analysis.

claim: The pipeline is expected to improve with general advancement in self-supervised deep learning.
source: Since our pipeline is based on the fast-evolving field of self-supervised deep learning, we expect it to further improve with its general advancement.
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements.

claim: Hardware improvement (GPU RAM size) is expected to allow training bigger models on larger texture patches of higher resolution that might further refine the quality of morphological representations.
source: Additionally, we expect hardware improvement, i.e., GPU RAM size, to allow training bigger models on larger texture patches of higher resolution that might further refine the quality of morphological representations.
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements.

claim: The modularity of the pipeline allows integration of data from other modalities such as transcriptomics, proteomics, or metabolomics.
source: Another interesting direction enabled by the modularity of our pipeline is to integrate data from other modalities. Our features currently integrate shape and texture information of cells, but one could also envision enriching cellular descriptions by adding different types of data, e.g., transcriptomics, proteomics, or metabolomics, in a similar manner.
evidence: This is a speculation about future extensions.

claim: The pipeline can enable fast systematic investigation of large EM volumes involving consistent grouping and characterisation of morphological types.
source: We envision our pipeline to enable, for the first time, fast systematic investigation of large EM volumes that involves consistent grouping and characterisation of morphological types, discovering particular phenotypes and neighbourhoods, as well as localising cells or tissues in an animal volume that are visually similar to cells or groups of cells of interest.
evidence: This is a speculation about applications.

claim: Training the pipeline on multiple volumes simultaneously could produce sample-independent features for mapping cells to their corresponding partners in another volume.
source: Moreover, we expect MorphoFeatures to be useful for studies where several image volumes of the same species are acquired, be it another sample, a varying phenotype, or a different developmental stage. In such cases, training the pipeline on multiple volumes simultaneously to produce sample-independent features would result in morphological representations that can be used to map cells to their corresponding partners in another volume, enabling unbiased comparative analysis at scale.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications.

claim: Fine texture descriptors could be used to locate patches with phenotypic characteristic signature or cells with distinct ultrastructure in unsegmented volumes.
source: In addition, in case the other volumes are not segmented, one could use the fine texture part of MorphoFeatures to locate patches with phenotypic characteristic signature or cells with distinct ultrastructure (e.g. muscles and secretory cells).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications.

claim: The pipeline can be adjusted for other types of data such as brain EM volumes where MorphoFeatures could supplement neuron skeleton features.
source: The presented pipeline can also be adjusted for other types of data. For example, since our analysis revealed a high variability in neuronal soma morphologies, it appears reasonable to also apply the pipeline to brain EM volumes, where MorphoFeatures could supplement neuron skeleton features for more precise neuronal morphology description.
evidence: This is a speculation about applications to other data types.

claim: The approach is expected to contribute to the analysis of cells in other volumetric modalities, such as X-ray holographic nano-tomography (Kuan et al., 2020).
source: We also expect the approach to contribute to the analysis of cells in other volumetric modalities, such as X-ray holographic nano-tomography (Kuan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation with citation.

claim: For light microscopy with membrane staining, the shape part of the MorphoFeatures pipeline is expected to be directly applicable.
source: For light microscopy with membrane staining, we expect the shape part of the MorphoFeatures pipeline to be directly applicable and a useful addition to existing analysis tools.
evidence: This is a speculation about applicability to other imaging modalities.

claim: The cell clusters identified in MorphoFeature space appear to come closest to genetically defined cell types.
source: Most importantly, the cell clusters identified in MorphoFeature space appear to come closest to genetically defined cell types, as demonstrated here, among others, for different types of mechano-sensory cells or cell types of the apical nervous system.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: MorphoFeatures unravel morphological cell types without a genetic match in the cell type atlas, likely due to limited coverage of the atlas.
source: Interestingly, the MorphoFeatures also unravel morphological cell types without a genetic match in the cell type atlas (such as the enteric neurons, see above). This is most likely due to the yet limited coverage of the atlas and expected to improve with the continuous addition of genes to the atlas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of a finding.

claim: Integration of single cell transcriptomics data will be highly rewarding to improve the match between morphological and molecularly defined cell types.
source: In particular, the integration of other multimodal omics datasets such as single cell transcriptomics data will be highly rewarding to improve the match between morphological and molecularly defined cell types, which is the ultimate aim of cell type characterisation and categorisation (Zeng and Sanes, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements with citation.

claim: The automated tissue detection equally processes the morphological similarities of constituting cells, enabling tissue separation even when morphological boundaries appear to be absent.
source: While the manual segmentation of tissues mostly relies on the detection of tissue boundaries, our automated tissue detection equally processes the morphological similarities of its constituting cells. This enables tissue separation even in cases where morphological boundaries appear to be absent, as is the case for the anterior and posterior dorsal ganglionic nuclei, which are lacking a clear boundary but are composed of morphologically different cell types that are also genetically distinct (Vergara et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes an advantage of the method with citation.

claim: MorphoFeatures will allow comparison and identification of corresponding cell types in datasets of the same species, but also between species, on purely morphological grounds.
source: For the first time, the MorphoFeatures will allow us to compare and identify corresponding cell types in datasets of the same species, but also between species, on purely morphological grounds.
evidence: This is a claim about the potential impact of the work.

claim: MorphoContextFeatures automatically recognise tissues and organs across entire bodies, opening up new perspectives in comparative anatomy.
source: Furthermore, the MorphoContextFeatures automatically recognise tissues and organs across entire bodies, opening up new perspectives in comparative anatomy.
evidence: This is a claim about the potential impact.

claim: Without previous knowledge, the method can obtain the full complement of tissues and organs for a given specimen and quantitatively compare them to those of other specimens.
source: Without previous knowledge, we can obtain the full complement of tissues and organs for a given specimen and quantitatively compare them to those of other specimens of the same or other species.
evidence: This describes a capability of the method.

claim: In combination with cell type-, tissue-, and organ-specific expression data, the method will enable identification of corresponding traits in an unbiased manner and with unprecedented accuracy.
source: In combination with cell type-, tissue-, and organ-specific expression data, this will enable us to identify corresponding traits in an unbiased manner and with unprecedented accuracy.
evidence: This is a claim about future applications.
